1.title: Logical Access Controls
1.text: Welcome to Module eight: Logical Access Controls. It covers the exam area three. Identity and Access Management. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. three point two Understand logical access controls: Principle of Least Privilege (Po L P). Separation of Duties (So D). Access control models. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: three. Identity and Access Management (I A M) Concepts (twenty percent). Exam format: an adaptive exam of one hundred to one hundred twenty-five questions in two hours; a score of seven hundred on a scale of one to one thousand passes. Validated against: the official I S C two C C exam outline.

1.title: Subjects, objects and access control
1.text: Subjects, objects and access control. Logical access controls decide who or what (the subject) may do which action on which resource (the object) in computer systems. (Locks and guards are physical controls.). Subject. The user, process or bot that asks for access. Object. The file, database or system being accessed. Access control list (A C L). A list of who may do what on an object. Implicit deny. If no rule allows it, the answer is no.

1.title: Principle of least privilege (PoLP)
1.text: Principle of least privilege (Po L P). Give each identity only the access it needs to do its job, and no more, for as short a time as needed. Need to know. Access to information only if the job requires it. Just-in-time access. Temporary elevation that expires. Why. A stolen or misused account can do less harm; mistakes have a smaller reach. Applies to. People, service accounts and A I bots alike. Exam tip: Least privilege is the default answer when a question asks how to limit damage from a compromised or careless account.

1.title: Separation of duties (SoD)
1.text: Separation of duties (So D). Split a critical task among two or more people so that no single person can complete it alone. Fraud then needs collusion. The person who creates a vendor is not the person who approves payments. One person cannot steal alone. A developer cannot deploy to production; operations does. Untested code is less likely. Related ideas: two-person control (two people act together), job rotation, mandatory vacation (fraud shows when someone else covers the job). Exam tip: Po L P limits how much; So D splits who. If a question says no single person should be able to complete the task, the answer is separation of duties.

1.title: Access control models
1.text: Access control models. The figure shows this: Five access control models and who decides access in each.

1.title: Access control models, continued
1.text: Access control models. Discretionary (D A C). Who decides: The owner of the object. How: The owner grants rights to others (flexible, easy to misuse). Mandatory (M A C). Who decides: The system, by policy. How: Labels (such as secret) and clearances must match; government and military. Role-based (R back). Who decides: Roles of the job. How: Users get permissions through roles (accountant, nurse).

1.title: Access control models, continued
1.text: Access control models. Attribute-based (A B A C). Who decides: Rules over attributes. How: Combines user, resource and environment (department, device, time, location). Rule-based. Who decides: Fixed rules. How: A rule applies to everyone, such as allow only eight:zero to eighteen:zero. Exam tip: D A C equals owner decides. M A C equals labels and clearances. R back equals job role. A B A C equals attributes. Rule-based equals fixed rules. Do not mix up role-based with rule-based.

1.title: Authentication strength and monitoring
1.text: Authentication strength and monitoring. Factors. Something you know, have, are; M F A uses two different kinds. Biometrics. Measured by false acceptance rate (F A R), false rejection rate (F R R) and the crossover error rate (C E R) where they are equal. Privileged access management (P A M). Extra control and recording of administrator accounts. Behavior analysis. Systems, often A I-assisted, spot impossible travel or unusual logins. Exam tip: A lower C E R means a more accurate biometric system. M F A needs different categories, not two passwords.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. An analyst needs read access to one report folder for a project that lasts one week. What is the best way to apply least privilege? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Give read access to that folder only, and remove it after the week. Least privilege means only the needed access, for the needed time.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A company wants the clerk who enters invoices to be different from the manager who approves payment. Which principle is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Separation of duties, which splits a critical task. Splitting a critical task between people is separation of duties.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. In a system, the owner of a file decides who else can read it. Which access control model is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Discretionary access control based on the owner. When the owner decides who gets access, the model is discretionary.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Access to a record is allowed only for doctors, from hospital devices, during work hours. Which model uses these attributes of user, device and time? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Attribute-based access control. Attribute-based access control combines attributes of the user, the resource and the environment.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. A document is labeled secret and only users with a secret clearance can open it, whatever the owner wants. Which model is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Mandatory access control enforced by the system. Labels and clearances enforced by the system are mandatory access control.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. A new accountant is given the permissions that all accountants have through a group. Which model is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Role-based access control through a role. Permissions assigned through a job role are role-based access control.

1.title: Recall Check 1
1.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. What does least privilege mean? Answer: Only the access needed to do the job, and no more. Question two. What does separation of duties prevent? Answer: One person completing a critical task alone, so fraud needs collusion. Question three. Which model lets the owner share access? Answer: Discretionary access control.

1.title: Recall Check 2
1.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. What is implicit deny? Answer: If no rule allows access, it is refused. Question five. What does A B A C use? Answer: Attributes of the user, resource and environment. Question six. What does a lower crossover error rate mean? Answer: A more accurate biometric system.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Po L P: minimum access, minimum time; need to know; just in time. So D: split a critical task; collusion needed; job rotation. Models: D A C owner, M A C labels, R back roles, A B A C attributes, rule-based fixed rules. Biometrics: F A R, F R R, C E R (lower is better). Default: implicit deny; privileged accounts under P A M. If this course is helping you, please subscribe to the channel and hit the bell icon, so you get a notification when the next video is out.
